context.heading: The God who never lies
context.body: Paul opens by calling God apseudēs, literally "un-lying," the one who cannot lie. The word sets up a sharp contrast with the Cretan reputation for lying in verse 12. The hope of eternal life is anchored in a God whose word cannot fail (Numbers 23:19; Hebrews 6:18).

context.heading: God's household manager
context.body: An oikonomos ("steward") was a household manager, often a trusted slave who ran an estate for its owner. Calling an overseer "God's steward" reminds him that the church is not his house and its people are not his property. He manages what belongs to Someone else and will answer to Him.

context.heading: Their own prophet said it
context.body: The line "Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons" is traditionally credited to Epimenides, a Cretan poet of around 600 BC whom Greeks regarded as a seer. Cretans were mocked for claiming Zeus's tomb was on their island, and "to Cretanize" became Greek slang for lying. Quoting their own prophet made the point hard to dismiss as an outsider's insult.

theology.title: A promise older than time
theology.body: Eternal life was promised by God "before time began" and revealed "at the appointed time" through preaching (vv. 2–3). God's plan of salvation was not improvised; it unfolds on His schedule (Galatians 4:4). Paul's ministry on Crete is one link in a chain God forged long before.

theology.title: Truth that produces godliness
theology.body: Paul serves "the knowledge of the truth that leads to godliness" (v. 1). For God, truth and life are never separated, which is why false teachers are exposed by their actions (v. 16). The God who is truth forms people who live truthfully.

application.title: Home tells the truth
application.body: An elder's household is examined because home is where character is hardest to fake. Churches debate exactly what "children who are believers" requires, but the principle of a well-ordered home is plain.
application.question: What would your family say is the gap between who you are at church and who you are at home?

application.title: Profit bends the message
application.body: The false teachers on Crete taught "for the sake of dishonorable gain." When ministry, content or advice starts serving income first, the message usually bends to fit.
application.question: Where might money be quietly shaping what you say or leave unsaid?

application.title: Actions confess too
application.body: "They profess to know God, but by their actions they deny Him." Faith claims are easy to make and hard to hide behind for long.
application.question: What would someone conclude about your God from watching your last week?

context.heading: Not pilfering
context.body: Household slaves often handled money and goods, and petty theft was a common stereotype. Nosphizō ("steal," "embezzle") is the word used of Ananias keeping back part of the sale price (Acts 5:2). By honest work, Christian slaves would "adorn" (kosmeō, root of "cosmetic") the teaching about God our Savior.

context.heading: Grace dawns
context.body: Epiphainō means to appear or shine into view, used of light dawning on those in darkness (Luke 1:79). Greeks used the related word epiphaneia for a god's visible appearance or an emperor's arrival in a city. Paul says God's grace "has appeared" in Christ's first coming, and believers await His "glorious appearance" (v. 13).

context.heading: Our great God and Savior
context.body: In "our great God and Savior Jesus Christ," one Greek article governs both nouns, which most scholars take to mean both titles describe one person, Jesus. That makes this one of the clearest New Testament statements that Jesus is God (compare 2 Peter 1:1; John 20:28). Inscriptions sometimes hailed rulers as "god and savior," but Paul gives those titles to Christ.

theology.title: Grace that trains
theology.body: Grace does not only pardon; it "instructs" us (paideuō, the word for raising a child) to renounce ungodliness and live sensible, godly lives (v. 12). God's free gift comes with a new way of life, not as payment for it. That is how Paul holds salvation by grace together with a call to good works.

theology.title: His own possession
theology.body: Christ gave Himself to redeem us and "to purify for Himself a people for His own possession" (v. 14). The phrase echoes God's words to Israel at Sinai (Exodus 19:5; Deuteronomy 14:2). The church shares Israel's calling to be God's treasured people, set apart and "zealous for good deeds."

theology.title: Living between two appearings
theology.body: The chapter is framed by two appearings: grace has appeared (v. 11), and believers await the appearance of glory (v. 13). Christian life is lived in between, shaped by what God has done and by what He has promised to do.

application.title: Find an older guide
application.body: Paul builds the church around generations teaching each other, older women training younger women and Titus modeling for young men. Older believers carry lived experience you will not find in a podcast.
application.question: Who older than you could you ask to teach you something about faith, marriage or work this month?

application.title: Make the gospel attractive at work
application.body: Slaves were told to adorn the teaching about God through honesty and reliability. Showing up on time and not padding an expense report can make Christian belief look beautiful to coworkers.
application.question: What small dishonesty at work have you stopped noticing?

application.title: No age outgrows self-control
application.body: Paul calls for sensible, self-controlled living from older men, older women, young women and young men alike. No stage of life graduates from the need.
application.question: Where is your self-control weakest right now: food, screens, words or spending?

context.heading: God's philanthropy
context.body: Philanthrōpia ("love for mankind") was a virtue praised in Greek kings, who advertised their generosity to subjects. Paul applies it to God our Savior, whose kindness "appeared" in Christ. Unlike royal propaganda, God's love for humanity was proven when Christ came for people who deserved nothing.

context.heading: A factious person
context.body: Hairetikos ("divisive") comes from a verb meaning "to choose" and describes someone who forms a faction around their own opinions. The word later came to mean "heretic," but here the focus is on divisiveness more than precise doctrine. Titus warns such a person twice, then has nothing more to do with them (v. 10).

context.heading: Zenas the lawyer, winter at Nicopolis
context.body: Zenas is a nomikos ("lawyer"), an expert in either Jewish or Roman law; scholars are not sure which. Paul planned to winter at Nicopolis (v. 12), probably the city on Greece's west coast, since sea travel largely shut down in winter. Titus is to supply travelers like Zenas and Apollos so they lack nothing.

theology.title: The whole Trinity saves
theology.body: Verses 4–6 name God our Savior, the Holy Spirit who renews, and Jesus Christ our Savior through whom the Spirit is poured out. Salvation is the work of one God in three persons, "not by the righteous deeds we had done" (v. 5). Christians differ on whether "the washing of new birth" refers directly to baptism or to the inner cleansing baptism pictures (compare Ezekiel 36:25–27), but all agree the Spirit does the renewing.

theology.title: Poured out abundantly
theology.body: The Spirit was "poured out on us abundantly" (v. 6), the language of Joel 2:28 fulfilled at Pentecost (Acts 2:17, 33). God does not measure out His Spirit sparingly. He gives lavishly to people who were once "foolish, disobedient, misled" (v. 3).

application.title: Remember who you were
application.body: Paul tells believers to show consideration to everyone, because "at one time we too were foolish." Forgetting your own past makes contempt for others easy.
application.question: Who do you look down on that resembles the person you used to be?

application.title: Courtesy online
application.body: Believers on Crete were told "to malign no one" and to show "full consideration to everyone," rulers included. Online, that is a countercultural move.
application.question: How would your posts and comments change if you treated everyone in them as someone God may yet save?

application.title: Meet pressing needs
application.body: Paul ends by telling believers to devote themselves to good works that "meet the pressing needs of others." Good works are not vague niceness; they are practical help for people who are actually stuck.
application.question: What practical need in someone's life could you actually meet this week rather than just notice?
